claim: Working memory has long been assumed to play a role in prioritization and planning, while bridging cross-temporal contingencies during action selection.
source: Working memory has long been assumed to play a role in prioritization and planning, while bridging cross-temporal contingencies during action selection.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical role of working memory in the literature, supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: Studies of working memory have mostly focused on memory for single components of an action plan, such as a rule or a stimulus, rather than management of all of these elements during planning.
source: However, studies of working memory have mostly focused on memory for single components of an action plan, such as a rule or a stimulus, rather than management of all of these elements during planning.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature on working memory research.

claim: Both full action plans were maintained as conjunctive representations during action preparation, regardless of priority.
source: We found that both full action plans were maintained as conjunctive representations during action preparation, regardless of priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: During output selection, the conjunctive representation of the high-priority action plan was more enhanced and readily selected as an output.
source: However, during output selection, the conjunctive representation of the high-priority action plan was more enhanced and readily selected as an output.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing differential activation patterns during the test phase.

claim: The strength of the high-priority conjunctive representation was associated with behavioral interference when the low-priority action was tested.
source: Furthermore, the strength of the high-priority conjunctive representation was associated with behavioral interference when the low-priority action was tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by the trial-by-trial correlation analysis between representation strength and behavioral outcomes.

claim: Multiple alternate upcoming actions were maintained as integrated representations and served as the target of post-encoding attentional selection mechanisms to prioritize and select an action from within working memory.
source: Thus, multiple alternate upcoming actions were maintained as integrated representations and served as the target of post-encoding attentional selection mechanisms to prioritize and select an action from within working memory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Guiding actions in a complex environment often involves specification and selection of multiple candidate plans.
source: Guiding actions in a complex environment often involves specification and selection of multiple candidate plans (Cisek, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Working memory is thought of as a core interface, both for assembling and maintaining task-relevant plans, as well as gating a subset of this information to use when actions become relevant.
source: To this end, working memory is thought of as a core interface, both for assembling and maintaining task-relevant plans, as well as gating a subset of this information to use when actions become relevant (Chatham and Badre, 2015; Myers et al., 2017; Kriete and Noelle, 2011; Frank and Badre, 2012; Badre and Frank, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Top-down prioritization and selection of the encoded information have been commonly recognized as a function of working memory.
source: Top-down prioritization and selection of the encoded information have been commonly recognized as a function of working memory (Souza and Oberauer, 2016; Gazzaley and Nobre, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Retrospectively directing attention to specific memories (e.g. via retro-cues) makes the targeted content more accessible for later retrieval and more resilient against interference, while increasing its neural decodability.
source: Retrospectively directing attention to specific memories (e.g. via retro-cues) makes the targeted content more accessible for later retrieval and more resilient against interference, while increasing its neural decodability (LaRocque et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2020; Ester et al., 2018; Levin et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior empirical work.

claim: Control over working memory has been studied mostly with regard to sensory representations (e.g. words, letters, symbols, faces, scenes, and so forth) that are independent from their prospective goals and actions.
source: However, although the primary function of working memory is to guide future actions rather than passively store past sensations (Miller et al., 2018; Olivers and Roelfsema, 2020; Nobre and Stokes, 2019), control over working memory has been studied mostly with regard to sensory representations (e.g. words, letters, symbols, faces, scenes, and so forth) that are independent from their prospective goals and actions (Myers et al., 2017; Heuer et al., 2020; van Ede, 2020).
evidence: This claim characterizes the existing literature and is supported by citations.

claim: A conjunctive representation binds critical task-relevant features—including not only the sensory representation (i.e. stimulus), but also the action rule (i.e. context) and response—into an integrated representation that uniquely couples sensory and motor information for a specific goal.
source: This conjunctive representation, also termed an event or task file, binds critical task-relevant features —including not only the sensory representation (i.e. stimulus), but also the action rule (i.e. context) and response—into an integrated representation that uniquely couples sensory and motor information for a specific goal (Mayr and Bryck, 2005).
evidence: This claim defines conjunctive representation and is supported by a citation.

claim: Several theories of cognitive control proposed that over the course of action planning, the formation of such an integrated representation is essential for an action to be executed.
source: Several theories of cognitive control proposed that over the course of action planning, the formation of such an integrated representation is essential for an action to be executed (Frings et al., 2020; Henson et al., 2014; Hommel, 2004; Logan, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple theoretical frameworks.

claim: Humans form conjunctive representations while preparing context-dependent actions.
source: Recent studies that applied a decoding analysis to the distributed pattern of EEG activity revealed that humans form such a conjunctive representation while preparing context-dependent actions (Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020; Takacs et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent empirical studies.

claim: The temporal trajectories of conjunctive representations were dissociable from other action representations.
source: The temporal trajectories of conjunctive representations were dissociable from other action representations, and their trial-to-trial fluctuation in strength strongly correlated with efficient action control (e.g. stopping of actions or transitions of action over trials) over and above other task-relevant representations (Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020; Rangel et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claim: Trial-to-trial fluctuation in strength of conjunctive representations strongly correlated with efficient action control over and above other task-relevant representations.
source: The temporal trajectories of conjunctive representations were dissociable from other action representations, and their trial-to-trial fluctuation in strength strongly correlated with efficient action control (e.g. stopping of actions or transitions of action over trials) over and above other task-relevant representations (Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020; Rangel et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claim: A conjunctive representation uniquely specifies the to-be-executed action.
source: Because a conjunctive representation uniquely specifies the to-be-executed action, it may be an efficient, output-oriented format for maintenance, prioritization, and retrospective selection of the planned actions for future behavior (Badre et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is a theoretical statement supported by a citation.

claim: Previous studies have focused on a single episode of action selection.
source: Yet, previous studies have focused on a single episode of action selection.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature.

claim: It is unknown whether more than one competing conjunctive representation can be maintained in parallel.
source: Thus, it is unknown whether more than one competing conjunctive representation can be maintained in parallel.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature.

claim: Participants prepared two independent actions with unique stimulus-response mappings and chose one of them as a final response based on a retrospective cue.
source: Participants prepared two independent actions with unique stimulus-response mappings and chose one of them as a final response based on a retrospective cue.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: One of the actions was, on average, more likely to be tested, encouraging selective prioritization of that action until output selection.
source: One of the actions was, on average, more likely to be tested, encouraging selective prioritization of that action until output selection.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in the current study.

claim: When the high-priority action was tested as opposed to the low-priority action, participants responded significantly faster.
source: When the high-priority action was tested as opposed to the low-priority action, participants responded significantly faster, F(1,23) = 40.31, MSE = 962, p<0.001, M=371 ms, SE = 8.7 ms for high priority and M=428 ms, SE = 8.7 ms for low priority
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: When the high-priority action was tested, participants produced fewer errors compared to when the low-priority action was tested.
source: and produced fewer errors, F(1,23) = 31.81, MSE <.001, p<0.001, M=.11, SE = .01 for high priority and M=.22, SE = .01 for low priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: A trial-wise adaptive cutoff (i.e. response deadline) was significantly shorter for high-priority action.
source: Likewise, a trial-wise adaptive cutoff (i.e. response deadline) was significantly shorter for high-priority action, F(1,23) = 33.72, MSE = 7479, p<0.001, M=823 ms, SE = 13 ms for high priority and M=968 ms, SE = 13ms for low priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Most errors were responses corresponding to the untested action plan rather than random responses.
source: Most errors were responses corresponding to the untested action plan rather than random responses.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of error types in the behavioral data.

claim: Swapping errors occurred at significantly higher probability when the low-priority action was tested.
source: Such swapping errors occurred at significantly higher probability when the low-priority action was tested, again consistent with participants prioritizing the high-priority action during maintenance, F(1,23) = 12.59, MSE <.001, p=0.002, M=.74, SE = .01 for high priority and M=.81, SE = .01 for low priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of error data.

claim: The behavioral results indicate that both of the required actions were prepared, yet the action associated with the high test probability was prioritized over the other action.
source: Therefore, the behavioral results indicate that both of the required actions were prepared, yet the action associated with the high test probability was prioritized over the other action.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data patterns.

claim: During the encoding phase, representations of two stimuli for each action were encoded.
source: During the encoding phase, a mixed-effect model revealed that representations of two stimuli for each action were encoded, t(1,23) = 7.45, beta = .183, 95% CI [.136.230] for high priority; t(1,23) = 6.92, beta = .168, 95% CI [.121.216] for low priority
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: Stimulus representations quickly decayed yet remained active during the preparation phase.
source: and they quickly decayed yet remained active during the preparation phase, t(1,23) = 3.65, beta = .036, 95% CI [.016.052] for high priority; t(1,23) = 3.20, beta = .017, 95% CI [.006.027] for low priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data over time.

claim: During the preparation phase, the cued rule context shared by both plans was specified and maintained robustly.
source: During the preparation phase, the cued rule context shared by both plans was specified and maintained robustly, t(1,23) = 6.59, beta = .144, 95% CI [.101.186].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: Distinguishable conjunctive representations for both required actions emerged during the preparation phase.
source: Furthermore, distinguishable conjunctive representations for both required actions emerged, t(1,23) = 2.61, beta = .142, 95% CI [.004.025] for high priority; t(1,23) = 2.10, beta = .008, 95% CI [0.001.016] for low priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: The information about required responses was not reliably decodable during the preparation phase.
source: In contrast, the information about required responses was not reliably decodable during the preparation phase, t(1,23) = –.514, beta = .002, 95% CI [–.010.006] for high priority; t(1,23) = –1.57, beta = –.008, 95% CI [–.017.002] for low priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: Before the test phase, none of the representations is significantly modulated by different test probability values.
source: Before the test phase, none of these representations is significantly modulated by different test probability values, t(1,23) <1.62, suggesting that neither action plan was selectively prioritized during preparation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: Action plans were maintained as conjunctive representations instead of response representations during the preparatory phase.
source: Yet, action plans were maintained as conjunctive representations instead of response representations during the preparatory phase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of decodable representations.

claim: Representations of individual features of high- and low-priority actions mostly became decodable only when they were cued as an output.
source: Although, on average, representations of individual features of high- and low-priority actions mostly became decodable only when they were cued as an output (Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Conjunctive representations were significantly modulated by the selection demand (i.e. cued as an output or not) dependent on their priority.
source: conjunctive representations were significantly modulated by the selection demand (i.e. cued as an output or not) dependent on their priority (Figure 4; see Table 2 for the main effects).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: High-priority items were more active than low-priority items when they were cued, but the reverse was the case when low-priority items were cued.
source: Specifically, high-priority items were more active than low-priority items when they were cued, but the reverse was the case when low-priority items were cued.
evidence: This claim is based on the pattern of results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The four-way interaction (priority × test type × representation type [conjunction vs. response], × time interval [1500–1850 ms vs. 1850–2100 ms]) is not significant for both stimulus-aligned data and response-aligned data.
source: We found that this four-way interaction (priority × test type × representation type [conjunction vs. response], × time interval [1500–1850 ms vs. 1850–2100 ms]) is not significant for both stimulus-aligned data, t(1,23) = 1.65, beta = .058, 95% CI [–.012.015] and response-aligned data, t(1,23) = –1.24, beta = –.046, 95% CI [–.128.028].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the timing of effects.

claim: The late-emerging interaction in the low-priority test condition was more likely due to a slow decline in the strength of the untested high-priority conjunction rather than late selection of the low-priority conjunction.
source: This caveat notwithstanding, however, further exploratory analysis suggests that the late-emerging interaction in the low-priority test condition was more likely due to a slow decline in the strength of the untested high-priority conjunction rather than late selection of the low-priority conjunction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on exploratory analysis of the temporal dynamics shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tested low-priority conjunction emerged early and was sustained when it was the tested action and declined when it was untested.
source: In particular, the tested low-priority conjunction emerged early and was sustained when it was the tested action and declined when it was untested (–226−86 ms relative to the response onset, cluster-forming threshold, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation analysis of the temporal dynamics.

claim: The high-priority conjunction remained active in its untested condition, declining even later than the low-priority conjunction.
source: Importantly, the high-priority conjunction also remained active in its untested condition, declining even later.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the temporal dynamics of representations.

claim: The strength of high- and low-priority conjunctions did not correlate with each other over trials across during the entire preparation and selection period.
source: We found that the strength of high- and low-priority conjunctions did not correlate with each other over trials across during the entire preparation and selection period, t(1,23) >–1.40 for all individual time samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of trial-by-trial representation strength.

claim: A similar two-way interaction of priority and test condition was observed for response representations but not for the stimulus representations.
source: Finally, a similar two-way interaction of priority and test condition was observed for response representations but not for the stimulus representations (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Not every action feature is boosted by the retro-cue, and the conjunction is one of the targets of attentional modulation for selective output gating.
source: In summary, then, these results indicate that not every action feature is boosted by the retro-cue, and the conjunction is one of the targets of attentional modulation for selective output gating.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results across different representation types.

claim: The two conjunctions can be maintained in a somewhat parallel manner, and prioritization modulates output gating, not necessarily preparatory activation.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that the two conjunctions can be maintained in a somewhat parallel manner, and prioritization modulates output gating, not necessarily preparatory activation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal dynamics and correlation patterns of the representations.

claim: Stronger representations of a stimulus, response, and conjunction of the high-priority action predicted faster and more accurate responses when that high-priority action was tested by the cue.
source: Specifically, stronger representations of a stimulus, response, and conjunction of the high-priority action predicted faster and more accurate responses when that high-priority action was tested by the cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Facilitatory effects of high-priority representations were diminished or reversed into interference when the low-priority item was tested as a function of the strength of the high-priority representation.
source: Such facilitatory effects were diminished or reversed into interference, when the low-priority item was tested as a function of the strength of the high-priority representation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: On trials when the low-priority action plan was cued, but the high-priority action plan was strong, this led to slower responses and more errors.
source: In other words, on trials when the low-priority action plan was cued, but the high-priority action plan was strong, this led to slower responses and more errors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: When the high-priority item was selected, the strength of all representations correlated with better behavior.
source: We note again that when the high-priority item was selected, the strength of all representations correlated with better behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on the pattern of results in Figure 5.

claim: With the low-priority item, only the strength of the conjunctive representation of the low-priority item was predictive of behavior when that action was cued.
source: In contrast, with the low-priority item, only the strength of the conjunctive representation of the low-priority item was predictive of behavior when that action was cued.
evidence: This claim is based on the pattern of results in Figure 5.

claim: There was no evidence of a relationship between the strength of the low-priority response or stimulus representation and behavior when the low-priority action was cued.
source: There was no evidence of this relationship for the strength of the low-priority response or stimulus representation.
evidence: This claim is based on the pattern of results in Figure 5.

claim: The strength of the representations of the low-priority action mostly did not interfere with selection of the other, high-priority action, except for the conjunction on RTs.
source: Furthermore, the strength of the representations of the low-priority action mostly did not interfere with selection of the other, high-priority action, except for the conjunction on RTs, although a quantitatively similar pattern was observed for the response representation.
evidence: This claim is based on the pattern of results in Figure 5.

claim: During selection for the output, the conjunction and response representations, but not stimulus representations, were selectively activated contingent on the priority and output gating demand of corresponding actions.
source: Taken together, during selection for the output, the conjunction and response representations, but not stimulus representations, were selectively activated (Figure 4) and influenced efficient response selection (Figure 5) contingent on the priority and output gating demand of corresponding actions.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the patterns in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Effects of priority and selection on representations were asymmetric such that representations of high-priority action tended to have a stronger impact on output selection.
source: These effects were asymmetric such that representations of high-priority action tended to have a stronger impact on output selection, suggesting prioritization is established during output gating.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the asymmetric pattern of effects observed in the data.

claim: An integrated control representation that incorporates a conjunction of task-relevant information may be critical for flexible action selection.
source: Theories of cognitive control posit that an integrated control representation that incorporates a conjunction of task-relevant information, such as goals, action rules, sensorimotor features, and rewards, may be critical for flexible action selection (Hommel, 2019; Frings et al., 2020; Logan, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Recent evidence has established the critical role of conjunctive representations in execution and control of responses.
source: And, indeed, recent evidence has established the critical role of conjunctive representations in execution and control of responses (Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020; Kikumoto et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent empirical work.

claim: If conjunctive representations function as basic building blocks of action preparation and selection one would expect that people can maintain multiple conjunctions in working memory, prioritize them based on their expected utility, and selectively output one or another as circumstances dictate.
source: If conjunctive representations function as basic building blocks of action preparation and selection one would expect that people can maintain multiple conjunctions in working memory, prioritize them based on their expected utility, and selectively output one or another as circumstances dictate.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from theoretical considerations.

claim: The current study found evidence both for simultaneous preparation of two conjunctive representations and for priority-modulated output gating of the conjunction that correspond with the currently targeted action.
source: We found evidence both for simultaneous preparation of two conjunctive representations and for priority-modulated output gating of the conjunction that correspond with the currently targeted action.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the current study.

claim: Conjunctive representations influence post-encoding output selection over and above the constituent representations.
source: Furthermore, we found that conjunctive representations influence post-encoding output selection over and above the constituent representations, which were consistently targeted by attentional selection throughout a trial to maintain, prioritize, and select an action from the candidates held in working memory.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the current study.

claim: Maintenance of sensory information for upcoming output selection concurrently transforms task-relevant sensory memories in a more action-oriented or proceduralized representational format.
source: Our results add to a growing body of evidence that maintenance of sensory information for upcoming output selection concurrently transforms task-relevant sensory memories in a more action-oriented or proceduralized representational format (Oberauer, 2009; Hommel, 2019; Brass et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current findings and citations to prior work.

claim: Preparing future context-dependent actions recruited conjunctive representations that comprise the unique action constellation for output even after responses are fully specified.
source: Preparing future context-dependent actions recruited conjunctive representations that comprise the unique action constellation for output even after responses are fully specified (Figures 1, 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the referenced figures.

claim: Several current theoretical proposals for working memory suggest that encoded sensory information is reconfigured to a use-optimized format when a memorandum is assigned a specific use or selected for output.
source: Moreover, several current theoretical proposals for working memory suggest that encoded sensory information is reconfigured to a use-optimized format when a memorandum is assigned a specific use or selected for output (such as by retro-cueing) (Myers et al., 2017; Nobre and Stokes, 2019; Orhan and Ma, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical proposals.

claim: Participants can retrospectively prioritize and select conjunction representations based on task demands.
source: Consistent with these hypotheses, we observed here that participants can retrospectively prioritize and select conjunction representations based on task demands.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings.

claim: Both action conjunctions were maintained throughout the delay, but responses were not specified until the test period.
source: Importantly, whereas both action conjunctions were maintained throughout the delay, we did not find evidence that the responses were specified until the test period.
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal dynamics of decodable representations.

claim: The integrated conjunctive representation is used as a format for holding planned actions in working memory, even when all information is available to specify the response.
source: Though we don't rule out that in certain tasks responses would be maintained without the full conjunction, our results provide evidence that the integrated conjunctive representation is used as a format for holding planned actions in working memory, even when all information is available to specify the response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of maintained representations.

claim: Response representations were detected less than 300 ms after the response is specified in previous studies that did not include a delay period.
source: However, our previous studies that did not include a delay period Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020; Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020 found that response representations were detected less than 300 ms after the response is specified.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Responses can be formed far faster than the maintenance period provided in this study.
source: This suggests that responses can be formed far faster than the maintenance period provided in this study.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior findings.

claim: Unlike prior studies that manipulate post-encoding selection from working memory, stimulus representations showed a relatively weak effect of priority and selection demand and less interference on behavior.
source: Notably, unlike prior studies that manipulate post-encoding selection from working memory (Griffin and Nobre, 2003; Souza and Oberauer, 2016; Ester et al., 2018), we observed that stimulus representations showed a relatively weak effect of priority and selection demand and a less of interference on behavior (Table 2; Figure 4; Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current findings with prior work.

claim: The discrepancy in stimulus representation effects may be partially driven by the fact that the sensory inputs were explicitly contextualized or transformed by the action rules for the task.
source: This may be partially driven by the fact that the sensory inputs were explicitly contextualized or transformed by the action rules for the task.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: The RSA regression approach allows direct testing of conjunctive representations competing against other constituent formats, such as the simple stimulus representations.
source: However, another mutually compatible account of this discrepancy is that our RSA regression approach allows us to directly test conjunctive representations competing against other constituent formats, such as the simple stimulus representations.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Conjunctive representations and response representations reflect the priority of planned actions during post-encoding selection.
source: Instead of other action features, our results showed conjunctive representations and response representations reflect the priority of planned actions during post-encoding selection.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding which representations show priority effects.

claim: More context-specific representations may be a better format to capture control processes for post-encoding selection of a planned action.
source: Consistent with recent theories that explained post-encoding priority effects by linking its informational content to associated actions through attention (Allport et al., 1987; Souza and Oberauer, 2016; Olivers and Roelfsema, 2020; González-García et al., 2020), these results suggest that more context-specific representations may be a better format to capture control processes for post-encoding selection of a planned action.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings in the context of prior theories.

claim: Optimal control of actions may recruit conjunctive representations that minimally defines relevant task states to encode response representations that execute actions.
source: Beyond prioritization and selection, optimal control of actions may recruit conjunctive representations that minimally defines relevant task states to encode response representations that execute actions (Todorov, 2004; McNamee and Wolpert, 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The importance of the integrated representation fits with recent theories about the geometry of task representations by nonlinear integration of information as a key computational mechanism for working memory and cognitive flexibility.
source: The importance of the integrated representation in our results also fits with recent theories about the geometry of task representations by nonlinear integration of information, wherein sensory and context signals are projected into a high-dimensional population code, as a key computational mechanism for working memory and cognitive flexibility (Fusi et al., 2016; Buschman, 2021; Badre et al., 2021; Jazayeri and Ostojic, 2021; Freund et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to theoretical frameworks supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in association cortex (e.g. prefrontal and parietal cortex) exhibit nonlinear mixed selectivity or coding of task feature information in a conjunctive manner.
source: Supporting this view, neurons in association cortex (e.g. prefrontal and parietal cortex) exhibit nonlinear mixed selectivity or coding of task feature information in a conjunctive manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by the general knowledge from neuroscience literature.

claim: At the population level, conjunctive coding aids behavioral flexibility by discriminating readout for diverse combinations of inputs.
source: At the population level, this coding aids behavioral flexibility by discriminating readout for diverse combinations of inputs (Rigotti et al., 2013; Parthasarathy et al., 2019; Bernardi et al., 2020; Panichello and Buschman, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claim: A recent model of working memory explicitly addressed conjunctive coding by task-agnostic random networks and highlighted their role in flexibly maintaining arbitrary inputs.
source: A recent model of working memory explicitly addressed conjunctive coding by task-agnostic random networks and highlighted their role in flexibly maintaining arbitrary inputs (Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a computational model.

claim: The flexible yet capacity-limited nature of working memory may originate from the interaction between a structured layer containing subnetworks of sensory features and an unstructured (random) layer responding to integrated information in high-dimensional spaces.
source: This model proposed that the flexible yet capacity-limited nature of working memory may originate from the interaction between a structured layer containing subnetworks of sensory features and an unstructured (random) layer responding to integrated information in high-dimensional spaces.
evidence: This claim describes a theoretical proposal from a cited model.

claim: The observed conjunctive representations during preparation of future actions may reflect a working memory system that maximizes flexibility by relying on integrative connections.
source: Perhaps consistent with these perspectives, the observed conjunctive representations during preparation of future actions may reflect a working memory system that maximizes flexibility by relying on integrative connections (Buschman, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the findings to theory.

claim: High-dimensional representations can cast multiple task features into separable patterns, which could reduce their overlap and mitigate task interference.
source: A further benefit of high-dimensional representations is that they can cast multiple task features into separable patterns, which could reduce their overlap and mitigate task interference (Musslick et al., 2020; Badre et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: When prioritized conjunctive representations were strong during the test phase, they interfere with selecting an alternate action (i.e. the low-priority action).
source: Yet, we observed that when prioritized conjunctive representations were strong during the test phase, they interfere with selecting an alternate action (i.e. the low-priority action), perhaps suggesting either that the separability between the two action plans was compromised or not complete.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral interference effects observed in the data.

claim: The interference may reflect downstream processes that must select between the action plans.
source: Though, it is also possible that the interference reflects downstream processes that must select between the action plans, as discussed below.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the interference effect.

claim: A context-dependent control mechanism that selectively gates into and out of working memory has been extensively studied.
source: A context-dependent control mechanism that selectively gates into and out of working memory has been extensively studied as one such mechanism (O Reilly and Frank, 2006; Hazy et al., 2022; Frank and Badre, 2012; Badre and Frank, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on gating mechanisms.

claim: The PBWM (prefrontal cortex basal ganglia working memory) model implements gating of working memory via dopaminergic reinforcement learning in basal ganglia nested within cortico-striatal hierarchical loops.
source: One computational account, named the PBWM (prefrontal cortex basal ganglia working memory) model, implements gating of working memory via dopaminergic reinforcement learning in basal ganglia nested within cortico-striatal hierarchical loops.
evidence: This describes a computational model from the literature.

claim: The computational architecture of the PBWM model provides a natural mechanism for combining values or expected utility of information into gating decisions.
source: The computational architecture of the PBWM model provides a natural mechanism for combining values or expected utility of information into gating decisions.
evidence: This describes a feature of the PBWM model.

claim: At the algorithmic level, the current study supports the use of selective output gating for action preparation.
source: At the algorithmic level, the current study supports the use of selective output gating for action preparation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in terms of computational mechanisms.

claim: The current results highlighted an active role of integrated representations in biasing prioritization and selection of the planned actions on behavior.
source: Yet, unlike previous studies focusing on the role of compositional representations of the task-relevant inputs (e.g. rule or context representations), our results highlighted an active role of integrated representations in biasing prioritization and selection of the planned actions on behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of the novel contribution of the current findings.

claim: Multiple action plans could be retrospectively selected from within working memory, albeit with interference costs from the prioritized action during output selection phase.
source: Our results showed that multiple action plans could be retrospectively selected from within working memory, albeit with interference costs from the prioritized action during output selection phase.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Within the PBWM framework, the interference effect could be accounted for by changes in expected value that occur after the 'GO!' cue modulating gating operations in the basal ganglia.
source: We note that within the PBWM framework, the interference effect could be accounted for by changes in expected value that occur after the 'GO!' cue modulating gating operations in the basal ganglia (e.g. changes in drift rate), which may occur regardless of the separability of cortical representations.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings in terms of the PBWM model.

claim: The late appearance of the priority effect and its interaction with selection demand suggest that output selection of a low-priority action may induce switching of output gate that propagates down to the conflict at motor gating.
source: The late appearance of the priority effect and its interaction with selection demand (Figure 4) and more pronounced interference effect of high-priority action features (Figure 5) suggest that output selection of a low-priority action may induce switching of output gate that propagates down to the conflict at motor gating.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal dynamics and interference patterns.

claim: The priority of actions is mainly reflected during gating operations for selecting one or another action.
source: From this perspective, the priority of actions is mainly reflected during gating operations for selecting one or another action.
evidence: This is an interpretation of when priority effects are expressed.

claim: Most errors were execution of the uncued actions.
source: Consistent with this view, most errors were execution of the uncued actions (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the error analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The high-priority conjunction is sustained until late, even when it is untested.
source: Furthermore, with the caveat that we do not have statistical evidence of that allows us to draw strong inferences about timing of gating operations over different representations (e.g. conjunctive and response representations) within the test phase, the pattern of the results suggests that the high-priority conjunction is sustained until late, even when it is untested.
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal dynamics of representations with a caveat about statistical evidence.

claim: The sustained pattern of the high-priority conjunction is notable in light of the observation that its strength interferes with behavior when the low-priority item is tested, but not vice versa.
source: This sustained pattern is notable in light of our observation that the strength of the high-priority conjunctive representation interferes behavior when the low-priority item is tested, but not vice versa.
evidence: This connects the temporal dynamics to the behavioral interference effects.

claim: Coactivation of high-priority and low-priority conjunctions could be the basis of conflict for circuits deciding what to gate, which produces a behavioral interference effect.
source: If verified, it is possible that this coactivation could be the basis of conflict for circuits deciding what to gate, which produces a behavioral interference effect.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the interference effect.

claim: The current study provided initial evidence that multiple future actions could be maintained as conjunctive representations, and this level of representation is a key target of processes that prioritize prepared actions and guide their retrospective selection.
source: Understanding cognitive flexibility requires answering how action plans are represented, maintained, prioritized, and selected based on changing circumstances in our environment. The current study provided an initial evidence that multiple future actions could be maintained as conjunctive representations, and this level of representation is a key target of processes that prioritize prepared actions and guide their retrospective selection.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: Twenty-six participants (16 females; mean age: 23.2 years) were recruited from the University of Oregon student body.
source: Twenty-six participants (16 females; mean age: 23.2 years) were recruited from the University of Oregon student body.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: After preprocessing the EEG data, two participants were removed and were not analyzed further due to excessive amounts of artifacts (i.e. more than 25% of trials).
source: After preprocessing the EEG data, two participants were removed and were not analyzed further due to excessive amounts of artifacts (i.e. more than 25% of trials; see EEG recordings and preprocessing for detail).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: For each trial, participants were instructed to prepare two possible actions for upcoming tests by applying the single shared rule to two independent stimuli.
source: For each trial, participants were instructed to prepare two possible actions for upcoming tests by applying the single shared rule to two independent stimuli (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the task instructions.

claim: The required two actions on each trial were selected from the shared action constellations or S-R mappings shown in Figure 1b.
source: The required two actions on each trial were selected from the shared action constellations or S-R mappings shown in Figure 1b.
evidence: This describes the task design with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: An adaptive cutoff was used to limit the test interval to encourage participants to prepare two actions before the final test period.
source: In order to encourage participants to prepare two actions before the final test period (starting 1500 ms after the stimulus, Figure 1a), an adaptive cutoff was used to limit the test interval.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the task design.

claim: The cutoff interval was initially defined as 1200 ms, then it was adaptively adjusted trial-to-trial by increasing the interval after any incorrect trials whereas decreasing the interval after five consecutive correct trials.
source: This cutoff interval was initially defined as 1200 ms, then it was adaptively adjusted trial-to-trial by increasing the interval after any incorrect trials whereas decreasing the interval after five consecutive correct trials.
evidence: This describes the adaptive algorithm for the response deadline.

claim: Expected test probability was cued by color of the bar stimuli (i.e. blue and green) to either a high (70%) or low (30%) test probability.
source: Expected test probability was cued by color of the bar stimuli (i.e. blue and green) to either a high (70%) or low (30%) test probability.
evidence: This describes the priority manipulation in the task.

claim: The assignment of color to test probability was randomized for every block, therefore, one action plan was always more likely to be tested than the other in all trials.
source: The assignment of color to test probability was randomized for every block, therefore, one action plan was always more likely to be tested than the other in all trials.
evidence: This describes the randomization procedure for the priority manipulation.

claim: Participants gained performance-based incentives only when the overall accuracy was above 85% in a given block.
source: To prevent participants from disregarding information related to the low-test probability action, participants gained performance-based incentives only when the overall accuracy was above 85% in a given block, which was difficult to achieve if they used such a strategy, given the speeding required by the adaptive cutoff.
evidence: This describes the incentive structure to ensure task compliance.

claim: There were two practice blocks and 180 experimental blocks.
source: There were two practice blocks and 180 experimental blocks.
evidence: This describes the number of blocks in the experiment.

claim: Scalp EEG activities were recorded using 20 tin electrodes on an elastic cap using the international 10/20 system.
source: We recorded scalp EEG activities using 20 tin electrodes on an elastic cap (Electro-Caps) using the international 10/20 system.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording setup.

claim: The scalp EEG and EOG were amplified with an SA Instrumentation amplifier with a bandpass of 0.01–80 Hz, and signals were digitized at 250 Hz.
source: The scalp EEG and EOG were amplified with an SA Instrumentation amplifier with a bandpass of 0.01–80 Hz, and signals were digitized at 250 Hz in LabView 6.1 running on a PC.
evidence: This describes the EEG signal acquisition parameters.

claim: Trial-to-trial epochs including blinks, large eye movements, or blocking of signals were excluded from subsequent analyses.
source: The trial-to-trial epochs including blinks (>250 μv, window size = 200 ms, window step = 50 ms), large eye movements (>1°, window size = 200 ms, window step = 10 ms), blocking of signals (range = –0.01–0.01 μv, window size = 200 ms) were excluded from subsequent analyses.
evidence: This describes the artifact rejection criteria for EEG data.

claim: Using artifact rejection criteria, 268 trials (15%) of trials in each subject on average were excluded.
source: Using these criteria, we excluded 268 trials (15%) of trials in each subject on average.
evidence: This reports the amount of data excluded due to artifacts.

claim: Temporal-spectral profiles of single-trial EEG data were computed via complex wavelet analysis.
source: Temporal-spectral profiles of single-trial EEG data were computed via complex wavelet analysis (Cohen, 2014) by applying time-frequency analysis to preprocessed EEG data epoched for the entire block (>27.5 s to exclude the edge artifacts).
evidence: This describes the time-frequency analysis method with a citation.

claim: The power spectrum was convolved with a series of complex Morlet wavelets, where frequency increased from 1 to 35 Hz in 35 logarithmically spaced steps.
source: The power spectrum was convolved with a series of complex Morlet wavelets, where t is the time, f is the frequency increased from 1 to 35 Hz in 35 logarithmically spaced steps, and σ defines the width of each frequency band, set according to n/2pft, where n increased from 3 to 10.
evidence: This describes the parameters of the wavelet analysis.

claim: Separate linear decoders were trained to classify all possible action constellations for each independently planned action at every sample in trial-to-trial epochs.
source: As the first step, separate linear decoders were trained to classify all possible action constellations (Figure 1b) for each independently planned action at every sample in trial-to-trial epochs.
evidence: This describes the decoding analysis approach.

claim: A penalized linear discriminant analysis was performed using the caret package in R.
source: Specifically, we performed a penalized linear discriminant analysis using the caret package in R (Hastie et al., 1995; Kuhn, 2008).
evidence: This describes the specific analysis method with citations.

claim: For each action, the 12 unique action constellations were defined by the combination of 3 rules and 4 stimulus positions.
source: For each action, the 12 unique action constellations were defined by the combination of 3 rules and 4 stimulus positions (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the classification categories with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Decoders were trained with the instantaneous power of rhythmic EEG activity, which was averaged within predefined ranges of frequency values, generating 100 data features (5 frequency-bands × 20 electrodes) for training.
source: Decoders were trained with the instantaneous power of rhythmic EEG activity, which was averaged within the predefined ranges of frequency values (1–3 Hz for the delta-band, 4–7 Hz for the theta-band, 8–12 Hz for the alpha-band, 13–30 Hz for the beta-band, 31–35 Hz for the gamma-band), generating 100 data features (5 frequency-bands × 20 electrodes) for training.
evidence: This describes the feature extraction for the decoder.

claim: A k-fold repeated, cross-validation procedure was used to evaluate the decoding results by randomly partitioning single-trial EEG data into four independent folds with equal number of observations of each action constellation.
source: We used a k-fold repeated, cross-validation procedure to evaluate the decoding results by randomly partitioning single-trial EEG data into four independent folds with equal number of observations of each action constellation.
evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure.

claim: RSA was performed on the graded classification probabilities to assess the underlying similarity structure.
source: We next performed RSA on the graded classification probabilities to assess the underlying similarity structure.
evidence: This describes the RSA analysis approach.

claim: Each RSA model matrix uniquely represents a potential, underlying representation (e.g. rules, stimuli, responses, and conjunctions), which makes unique predictions for different action plans.
source: Each RSA model matrix uniquely represents a potential, underlying representation (e.g. rules, stimuli, responses, and conjunctions), which makes unique predictions for different action plans.
evidence: This describes the RSA model design.

claim: For independent decoding results of each of the action plans, the vector of logit-transformed classification probabilities was regressed onto RSA model vectors.
source: Specifically, for independent decoding results of each of the action plans, we regressed the vector of logit-transformed classification probabilities onto RSA model vectors.
evidence: This describes the RSA regression procedure.

claim: All model vectors were regressed simultaneously to estimate the unique variance explained by competing models, resulting in coefficients for each of the four model vectors.
source: To estimate the unique variance explained by competing models, we regressed all model vectors simultaneously, resulting in coefficients for each of the four model vectors.
evidence: This describes how unique variance was estimated for each representation type.

claim: Subject-specific regressors of z-scored, average RTs, and accuracies in each action constellation were included to reduce potential biases in decoding of conjunctions.
source: We also included subject-specific regressors of z-scored, average RTs, and accuracies in each action constellation to reduce potential biases in decoding of conjunctions.
evidence: This describes a control for potential confounds in the analysis.

claim: Multilevel models were used to assess the decoded representations and relate them to trial-to-trial variability in behavior.
source: We used multilevel models to further assess the decoded representations (Figure 4; Table 1) and relate them to trial-to-trial variability in behavior (Figure 5).
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling approach.

claim: Non-parametric permutation tests were used to evaluate the decoding results in the time domain.
source: For the results of time-resolved regression (Figure 4), we used non-parametric permutation tests to evaluate the decoding results in the time domain (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This describes the statistical testing approach with a citation.
